questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: State what makes an organisation a political party
questions.stem: Mistake M-01: The draft says a party is any group of people who agree politically, and the editor needs the claim repaired.

options.text: A party is a durable organisation with a programme and a common label, not merely an agreement
A party is any collection of voters who share the same preference at one election
options.misconception: treats a single electoral preference as an organisation

options.text: A party is best described as a set of ideas that compete for influence in the legislature
options.misconception: reduces a party to its programme and drops its organisation

options.text: A party is a body formed only after the constitution is drafted and approved
options.misconception: ties the existence of parties to a constitutional moment

questions.explanation: The error is that it drops organisation and continuity, leaving only shared opinion. A party combines a name, a programme and durable structures that contest elections over time.
questions.hint: Ask what makes a party more than shared opinion.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Define a party system in terms of the pattern of competition
questions.stem: Common error E-14: The draft treats the party system as the list of parties in the legislature, and the reviewer must explain the correct idea.

answer.exemplar: The party system is not the roster of parties but the stable pattern of competition they form together, including which parties are plausible contenders and how the main ones relate to one another. A roster describes membership of one institution at one moment, while the system describes the structure of competition that persists over time. A new party matters to the system if it changes that structure, not simply if it adds a line to the list.

questions.explanation: A system is a pattern of competition that endures, not a list of bodies in one chamber. The roster can change without the system changing, and the system can change without the roster changing much.
questions.hint: Ask whether the definition describes a pattern or a list.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Classify a competition system from vote shares

stimulus.body: Across three elections the leading party took 41, 44 and 39 per cent of the vote, while the second party took 30, 31 and 33 per cent. Two other parties each held between 8 and 12 per cent throughout, and a new party took 9 per cent in the third election.

questions.stem: Misreading R-27: The note says competition in this country is single-party, and the correction must be grounded in the vote figures.

options.text: Competition is single-party because three parties reached double figures
options.misconception: treats small parties as proof of one-party rule

options.text: The leading party dominates without a majority, and a strong second party keeps the contest competitive
Competition is single-party because the leader wins every election outright
options.misconception: confuses a clear leader with the absence of any real contest

options.text: Competition is single-party because no other party ever exceeds 10 per cent
options.misconception: ignores the second party's thirty per cent block of votes

questions.explanation: No party reaches a majority and one competitor holds around a third of the vote, so this is competitive rather than one-party. The label follows the pattern of competition.
questions.hint: Ask whether any single party can govern alone.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain voter convergence without claiming party agreement

stimulus.body: In a survey of voters in four districts, the gap in support between the two leading parties narrowed in every district where both had run strong local candidates. It widened in districts where only one of them had done so.

questions.stem: Claim to fix F-08: The draft says two parties in this system do not really differ, and the correction must use the survey evidence.

options.text: Voters see no difference because both parties use the same campaign slogan
options.misconception: substitutes campaign style for the voter's reasoning

options.text: The narrow gap shows voters have stopped caring which party wins
options.misconception: reads convergence in alignment as indifference to outcomes

options.text: The parties differ in policy, but strong local candidates can make voters treat them as similar
The parties are identical because both advocate the same economic programme
options.misconception: invents identical programmes without any evidence

questions.explanation: The survey links convergence to strong local candidates, a perception effect rather than proof the parties are identical. Convergence does not show indifference, and slogans are not mentioned.
questions.hint: Ask what the survey actually varied.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain how fragmentation produces coalition government
questions.stem: Confusion X-33: The draft asks how a fragmented parliament produced a stable government, and the reviewer wants a coherent answer.

options.text: Fragmentation produces stability because voters reward parties that refuse to cooperate
options.misconception: invents an electoral reward for refusing to cooperate

options.text: A fragmented parliament is stable because each small party holds the balance of power
options.misconception: treats a blocking position as if it supplied a majority

options.text: Fragmentation ends when the largest party decides to govern without allies
options.misconception: assumes a government can be stable without support

options.text: Fragmentation pushes parties toward combination, since no single party can assemble a working majority

questions.explanation: With no majority for any single party, combination is the only route to governing, so fragmentation produces coalitions rather than stability. Balancing power cannot assemble a government.
questions.hint: Ask how a government can be assembled at all.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain what a party contributes beyond any single candidate
questions.stem: Slip to correct S-19: The draft describes parties as merely vehicles for candidates, and the fix must restore what parties add.

options.text: Parties offer voters a label and a set of commitments that survive the fortunes of one candidate
Parties add nothing, since every candidate speaks for themselves alone
options.misconception: assumes parties add nothing to the candidates they contain

options.text: Parties exist only to organise the counting of votes on election day
options.misconception: reduces parties to administrative helpers on polling day

options.text: Parties are useful mainly for hiring staff after the results are known
options.misconception: invents a post-election staffing function for the party

questions.explanation: Parties supply continuity, a label and a programme that outlive any candidate, letting voters judge them across elections. Counting votes and hiring staff are administrative.
questions.hint: Ask what a party offers that one candidate cannot.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain the direction of travel of mass party membership
questions.stem: False premise P-02: The draft assumes parties in this period grew through membership, and the note must correct the direction of travel.

answer.exemplar: The premise is backwards for the period described. Party membership, once measured in millions of paying members organised in local branches, declined steadily while electoral support remained broadly stable. The organisation therefore became a thinner instrument: fewer members, less funding from dues, weaker local presence and fewer people available for canvassing. Parties adapted by shifting work towards candidates, professional campaign staff and paid communication rather than by recruiting more members.

questions.explanation: The draft reverses the trend: membership fell while vote shares held, so the organisation weakened without losing elections. Adapting through staff rather than membership is what it misses.
questions.hint: Ask whether membership grew or shrank.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Name the strategy of appealing across the political spectrum

stimulus.body: One party dropped its explicit commitment to a single economic programme, widened the range of policy positions it would accept and campaigned on several issues at once. Its vote share rose among voters who had previously described themselves as independents.

questions.stem: Gloss X-11: The note describes a party broadening its platform, and the correction must name the strategy involved.

options.text: The party adopted a regional strategy aimed at particular provincial strongholds
options.misconception: infers a geographic focus where the note describes breadth

options.text: The party adopted a catch-all strategy, seeking votes beyond a narrow ideological constituency
The party adopted a class-based strategy aimed squarely at working voters
options.misconception: reads a broad appeal as an appeal aimed at one social class

options.text: The party adopted an ideological strategy by concentrating on one clear position
options.misconception: confuses dropping one commitment with concentrating on one

questions.explanation: Dropping a narrow commitment and appealing to former independents is the signature of a catch-all strategy. Nothing in the note concerns class, ideological purity or provincial strongholds.
questions.hint: Ask what the party was trying to widen.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Enumerate the range of functions a party performs

stimulus.body: The party organisation recruits candidates, registers voters, publishes a programme, raises funds, canvasses for members of parliament and runs election-day logistics. It also fields candidates for local councils and, in one region, for a directly elected regional body.

questions.stem: Common error E-27: The draft lists only candidate recruitment and calls that the whole of a party's function.

options.text: The other activities belong to government, so parties only need to nominate candidates
options.misconception: assigns programme and mobilisation work to the wrong body

options.text: The party is a temporary body formed for each election and dissolved afterwards
options.misconception: contradicts the continuous organisation the note describes

options.text: Recruitment is one function among several, spanning participation, programme, funding and mobilisation
Recruitment is the core function, and the other activities are its necessary means
options.misconception: reduces a wide set of functions to one dominant activity

questions.explanation: The note describes continuing functions including programme, funding, registration and mobilisation, not only recruitment. Parties are continuous bodies, so the claim is unfounded.
questions.hint: Count the functions the note actually lists.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Separate the idea of a party system from the holding of elections
questions.stem: Misreading R-44: The draft says two countries both have a party system because both hold elections, and the fix must separate the concepts.

options.text: Elections and party systems are the same thing under different names in political science
options.misconception: collapses two distinct concepts into a single synonym

options.text: A party system exists wherever there are parties, however they relate to one another
options.misconception: reduces a system to its components, dropping the relations

options.text: Party systems are irrelevant to analysis, since elections alone explain voting behaviour
options.misconception: dismisses a foundational concept as irrelevant

options.text: Elections are a feature of the system, but the system is the pattern of competition the parties form

questions.explanation: Elections occur under many party arrangements, so they cannot define a system. The system is the enduring pattern of competition, of which elections are one recurring feature.
questions.hint: Ask whether elections can occur without a system.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish one-party systems from systems with a dominant party
questions.stem: Confusion X-45: The draft claims a country is a one-party system because one party always wins, and the correction must address the claim.

options.text: Winning often is not the same as being alone, because competition requires viable alternatives
If one party always wins, the country is a one-party system by definition
options.misconception: treats repeated victory as proof that no competition exists

options.text: A one-party system exists wherever a single party is the largest in every election
options.misconception: confuses being the largest party with being the only party

options.text: One-party systems only exist in countries that forbid all other organisations
options.misconception: narrows the definition to one organisational prohibition

questions.explanation: A one-party system means the absence of meaningful alternatives, not that one party tends to win. Where credible rivals exist and can displace the leader, competition remains.
questions.hint: Ask whether other parties could win.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish convergence in voting from agreement in policy
questions.stem: Patch note N-25: The draft equates two-party convergence with agreement on policy, and the reviewer wants the correction written out.

answer.exemplar: Convergence describes voters moving toward one another in their party choice, not the parties adopting the same policies. Two parties can attract increasingly similar voters while offering clearly different programmes, in which case the choice between them narrows even as the differences remain. The draft therefore mistakes a shift in the distribution of votes for a shift in the content of party platforms, and the two should be examined with separate evidence.

questions.explanation: Convergence concerns where voters go, not what parties say. Parties can become interchangeable to voters while their programmes diverge, so evidence about each is needed.
questions.hint: Ask whether the claim is about voters or policies.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain a coalition formed by parties with conflicting commitments

stimulus.body: After an election in which no party held more than 24 per cent, three parties that together held 41 per cent signed an agreement and a government was formed within a week. Two of the parties in the agreement had previously campaigned against each other on a constitutional question, and the third had publicly ruled out the government in question.

questions.stem: Claim to fix F-19: The draft says the coalition is surprising because these parties are ideologically incompatible, and the correction must use the note.

options.text: The coalition proves that electoral percentages alone determine which parties can govern
options.misconception: assumes seat numbers settle the question of who can govern

options.text: The arrangement is a pragmatic combination of parties that needed each other to govern
The coalition contradicts the note, because the parties had already agreed publicly on all major issues
options.misconception: claims a prior agreement the note does not record

options.text: The coalition shows the parties are more compatible than the note suggests they are
options.misconception: reads a pragmatic deal as evidence of ideological agreement

questions.explanation: The note shows parties that differed publicly combining because none could govern alone, the expected logic of a fragmented parliament. That is a pragmatic arrangement, not shared ideology.
questions.hint: Ask why each party joined.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Show how party organisation and candidate effort combine in a result

stimulus.body: In a constituency where the party selected a well-known local figure rather than a candidate from the national list, the party's vote rose from 14 to 27 per cent while the national vote of the same party fell slightly across the country. The constituency branch had kept its own list of preferred candidates for three decades.

questions.stem: Common error E-38: The draft says parties are irrelevant to elections because candidates do the work, and the fix must use the evidence.

options.text: The party lost votes nationally because the constituency result was won by the candidate
options.misconception: reverses the direction of the national and local figures

options.text: The constituency branch was unusual, so the result says nothing about party organisation
options.misconception: dismisses a case that is direct evidence about the mechanism

options.text: The candidate explains the result, but the party supplied the local organisation that chose and backed them
The evidence shows candidates matter and parties matter nothing at all in the outcome
options.misconception: draws a general conclusion from one constituency's outcome

questions.explanation: The party selected and supported the candidate through a long-standing local structure, so it was present in the result rather than incidental to it. The national fall does not make it irrelevant.
questions.hint: Ask who chose the candidate.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Assess what falling membership shows about party organisation
questions.stem: Slip to correct S-38: The draft argues that falling membership shows parties are finished, and the reviewer wants a fair assessment.

options.text: Declining membership proves parties are in terminal decline across every democracy
options.misconception: generalises a trend into an absolute claim about every case

options.text: Declining membership means parties now have no role in linking voters to government
options.misconception: concludes a total absence of function from a change in form

options.text: Declining membership shows that voters prefer independent candidates in every election
options.misconception: infers a uniform voter preference from one trend

options.text: Declining membership shows the classic mass party model has weakened, not that the party has disappeared

questions.explanation: The decline describes a party form, not the institution: parties reorganised around candidates, professional staff and paid media. What weakened is one way of organising politics.
questions.hint: Ask what exactly has declined.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Correct a reversed description of the catch-all strategy
questions.stem: Defect D-16: The draft lists the catch-all party as one that focuses tightly on a single policy, which reverses the concept.

options.text: A catch-all party seeks votes across the political spectrum rather than consolidating one position
A catch-all party campaigns on one policy in order to hold a narrow and loyal base
options.misconception: confuses a catch-all strategy with a narrow concentrated one

options.text: A catch-all party avoids elections and operates only between them as a pressure group
options.misconception: invents a non-electoral operating model for the party

options.text: A catch-all party wins by taking the votes of the single largest ideological group
options.misconception: reduces a broad appeal strategy to one constituency

questions.explanation: Catch-all means breadth, a deliberate attempt to appeal beyond a narrow base. Concentrating on one policy is the opposite of the strategy, and the term implies nothing about avoiding elections.
questions.hint: Ask whether the party seeks breadth or depth.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Replace an overstated claim about what a party represents
questions.stem: Repair R-11: The draft says parties represent the whole of society, and the reviewer wants a more defensible statement.

answer.exemplar: The claim overstates what a party can be shown to do. Parties aggregate and represent interests, but no party speaks for the whole of society, and the claim becomes less credible the more precisely it is asserted. A defensible formulation is that parties offer a way for organised interests to compete for influence and for voters to choose among coherent alternatives. Even this must be qualified by the fact that turnout and mobilisation differ sharply across groups, so some interests are represented more effectively than others.

questions.explanation: Parties aggregate and contest interests, and no party can be shown to represent society as a whole. Replace the claim with one about how interests are aggregated and offered as choices.
questions.hint: Ask whether any party can stand for everyone.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain how the same party can occupy different positions in two systems

stimulus.body: Two countries share a large party that wins roughly 30 per cent of the vote in both. In the first, that party is a plausible government and regularly forms coalitions after elections. In the second, the same party is treated by other parties as outside the mainstream and has never been invited to negotiate.

questions.stem: Gloss X-19: The note describes the same party playing different roles, and the correction must explain why.

options.text: The difference proves vote share has no bearing on a party's standing
options.misconception: ignores the repeated finding that vote share shapes standing

options.text: The party occupies different positions in the two systems, and its role depends on how others treat it
The party must have different policies in the two countries, since the behaviour differs
options.misconception: assumes identical vote share requires different programmes

options.text: Party roles are fixed by constitution, so the difference reflects written rules alone
options.misconception: attributes conduct to written rules without evidence of any

questions.explanation: The note attributes the difference to how other parties treat the party, a feature of each system rather than of the party. Identical vote shares can occupy different positions.
questions.hint: Ask who treats the party as an outsider.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish a shrunken opposition from an absent one

stimulus.body: The governing party in this country has held office for three consecutive terms and faces no unified alternative. A smaller party that once polled at 22 per cent now polls at 4 per cent and has lost all its members of parliament, and the two parties that remain differ from the government on only a few policies.

questions.stem: Misreading R-55: The draft says the country is a one-party system because one party dominates, and the fix must use the note.

options.text: The system should be classified as one-party because the opposition cannot win seats
options.misconception: equates the weakness of rivals with their legal absence

options.text: The system is fully competitive because the opposition differs on several policies
options.misconception: mistakes policy difference for the capacity to take office

options.text: The absence of a viable alternative lets one party dominate, which is dominance without a one-party system
With two opposition parties present, the country clearly has a competitive two-party system
options.misconception: counts parties without asking whether they can win

questions.explanation: A one-party system requires the absence of meaningful alternatives; here they exist but have been reduced to insignificance. That produces dominance, not the elimination of party competition.
questions.hint: Ask whether credible alternatives remain.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Treat convergence as concentration of choice rather than its loss
questions.stem: Confusion X-36: The draft treats two-party convergence as proof that democracy has become a two-party show, and the reviewer wants a proper treatment.

options.text: Convergence proves that voters no longer care about the differences between parties
options.misconception: infers indifference from a change in the vote distribution

options.text: Convergence means the two parties have abandoned their programmes and now agree on everything
options.misconception: assumes voting convergence implies policy agreement

options.text: Convergence is a permanent feature of every two-party democracy and cannot be reversed
options.misconception: assumes a pattern seen in one period is permanent everywhere

options.text: Convergence describes voters concentrating on two parties, which narrows preferences without removing them

questions.explanation: Convergence means support concentrates on fewer parties, compressing choice without removing differences between voters or programmes. It can reverse, and says nothing about what parties believe.
questions.hint: Ask what concentrates and what remains.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: State the general condition that makes coalition government necessary
questions.stem: Slip to correct S-47: The draft says coalitions arise only when no party has a majority, and the correction must state the general condition.

options.text: Coalitions are the general route to governing when the arithmetic of seats prevents any single majority
Coalitions form only in parliaments with more than three parties present
options.misconception: links coalition formation to party numbers, not to seats

options.text: Coalitions are a constitutional requirement in every parliamentary system
options.misconception: treats a constitutional convention as the trigger for deals

options.text: Coalitions appear only when a government is dissolved and re-elected
options.misconception: confines coalition practice to one procedural moment

questions.explanation: A coalition is the normal response to a fragmented arithmetic of seats, not to one procedural trigger or a fixed constitutional rule. The draft's condition is too narrow.
questions.hint: Ask what makes combining necessary.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain the relationship between a party and the candidate it promotes
questions.stem: False premise P-13: The draft treats party and candidate as rival explanations for an electoral result, and the reviewer wants the relationship explained.

answer.exemplar: Party and candidate are not competing explanations; in practice the candidate is normally selected and advanced by the party, and the party's label, machinery and programme travel with the candidate to the constituency. The candidate supplies local presence and personal appeal, while the party supplies continuity, resources and a national identity that helps the candidate be recognised. A result attributed to one of them has usually been produced by the combination, and the useful question is how much each contributed rather than which alone was decisive.

questions.explanation: The draft sets party and candidate against each other when the party normally selects, backs and brands the candidate. The productive question is how the two contributions combine.
questions.hint: Ask who selected and backed the candidate.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish organisational decline from electoral decline

stimulus.body: A party's membership roll fell from 340,000 to 96,000 over fifteen years while its vote share moved within a few points. Dues income dropped by two thirds, most local branches closed, and the number of volunteer canvassers per constituency fell from forty to six.

questions.stem: Common error E-49: The draft says the party has become electorally weaker, and the fix must use the note.

options.text: The note shows the party has ceased to function as an organisation at all
options.misconception: overstates a loss of capacity as the end of the organisation

options.text: Electorally the party has held its position, while its organisational capacity to campaign has fallen sharply
The party has clearly become weaker, because a falling membership always means falling support
options.misconception: equates organisational decline with a change in votes

options.text: The party has clearly become stronger, because membership was never relevant to elections
options.misconception: dismisses the link between organisation and campaigning

questions.explanation: Vote share barely moved while membership, dues and canvassers fell, so the loss is organisational rather than electoral. Campaigning capacity has shrunk sharply even though support has been stable.
questions.hint: Compare the vote figures with the organisation figures.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Show that broadening a programme need not dissolve a party's identity

stimulus.body: A party abandoned its traditional defence of a minimum wage and accepted a mixed package combining tax cuts with higher spending on health. Its support among union members, small business owners and graduates all rose at the same time, and it won more votes in every region of the country.

questions.stem: Claim to fix F-26: The draft says a party that changes its programme has abandoned its identity, and the correction must use the note.

options.text: Rising support across three groups proves the party has stopped representing anyone
options.misconception: treats broad appeal as the loss of any coherent constituency

options.text: The note proves the party's old programme was never genuinely held
options.misconception: infers the old position was insincere from a later change

options.text: Broadening a programme can attract voters across groups, so changing positions need not abandon a party
A party that changes its programme has broken its contract with its members
options.misconception: assumes a fixed programme is a binding moral commitment

questions.explanation: A catch-all strategy mixes positions to appeal across groups, so a shift in platform can widen support rather than dissolve the party's identity. The note suggests no insincerity.
questions.hint: Ask what happened to support after the change.

questions.learningObjective: Synthesise what a party does that a single candidate cannot
questions.stem: Confusion X-48: The draft asks what a party does for voters that a single candidate cannot, and the reviewer wants a synthesis.

options.text: A party competes in elections, while a candidate merely appears on the ballot on election day
options.misconception: reduces the candidate to one day rather than a campaign role

options.text: A party's main function is to select candidates, and everything else follows from that task
options.misconception: collapses several functions into selection alone

options.text: A party mainly provides a forum for debate, since elections can be contested without one
options.misconception: treats debate as the party's essential purpose

options.text: A party turns scattered preferences into a durable label and keeps resources between elections

questions.explanation: The distinctive contributions are continuity, aggregation and capacity: a persistent label, candidates chosen in advance, resources kept between elections. Selection is one part only.

questions.learningObjective: Sharpen a definition of the party system beyond a roster of names
questions.stem: Patch note N-33: The draft says the party system is simply all the parties that exist at a given time, and the correction must sharpen the definition.

options.text: The party system is the settled pattern of competition among the main parties, not a roster of names
The party system is the list of parties registered with the electoral commission
options.misconception: substitutes a legal register for a pattern of competition

options.text: The party system is the constitution, because the constitution establishes the parties
options.misconception: treats the constitution as a description of the system

options.text: The party system is the outcome of the most recent election, counted by seats won
options.misconception: confuses the current balance of forces with the system

questions.explanation: A system is the stable pattern of competition, so the definition must capture relations and durability rather than a list. A register, a constitution and one result are different things.
questions.hint: Ask whether the definition captures a pattern.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: State properly what distinguishes a one-party system from dominance
questions.stem: Repair R-30: The draft treats a single-party system as one where one party always wins, and the reviewer wants the concept stated properly.

answer.exemplar: The distinction the draft misses is between a party that dominates and a system in which only one party can exist. A one-party system is defined by the exclusion of alternatives, whether through law, administrative control of candidates or the absence of any organisation capable of challenging. Where a single party wins repeatedly because rivals are weak, the system remains plural and competitive, even if the outcome is predictable. stimulus.body: A survey of coalition governments in two dozen countries found that coalitions which included two parties that had previously competed for the same voters lasted longer on average than coalitions between parties drawing on distinct social groups. The same survey found no difference in their legislative output.

questions.stem: Gloss X-38: The note reports how coalition stability and legislative output differ, and the correction must be precise.

options.text: The survey proves that voter overlap makes coalitions unstable in every case
options.misconception: turns a difference between averages into a universal rule

options.text: Some coalitions last longer without producing more legislation, so duration and output must be told apart
Coalitions between rival parties last longer because they agree on more policy
options.misconception: reverses the direction of the duration finding

options.text: Coalitions that last longer necessarily legislate more, since longevity increases output
options.misconception: assumes duration causes legislative output

questions.explanation: The survey separates two measures: some coalitions survive longer while producing no more legislation, so stability and output must be reported apart. An average difference is not a law.
questions.hint: Ask what the two measures actually show.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Interpret a change of party name without substance behind it

stimulus.body: A party renamed itself and changed its logo before an election, then campaigned on a platform identical to the previous year's and fielded most of the same candidates in the same seats. Its vote share moved by less than one point.

questions.stem: Misreading R-29: The note describes a party changing its outward identity, and the correction must interpret it.

options.text: The identical platform proves the party had never needed a name to win votes
options.misconception: draws a sweeping claim from a single naming decision

options.text: The vote movement shows voters respond strongly to changes in presentation
options.misconception: reads a very small movement as a strong response

options.text: The party preserved its organisation and programme, so the rename altered appearance rather than substance
The rename shows the party had abandoned its programme and built something new
options.misconception: reads a change of name as a change of substance

questions.explanation: The platform and candidates stayed the same, so the rename changed the label rather than the organisation or programme, and the vote barely moved. Presentation is not substantive renewal.
questions.hint: Ask what did not change.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Assess the claim that parties must rebuild mass membership to survive
questions.stem: Confusion X-46: The draft says parties must rebuild mass membership or they will disappear, and the reviewer wants a fair assessment.

options.text: Parties without mass members have already disappeared from every democracy
options.misconception: turns a conditional claim into a universal historical fact

options.text: Only parties with mass membership can win elections in modern democracies
options.misconception: asserts a universal condition for electoral success

options.text: Mass membership was always a legal requirement for contesting elections
options.misconception: invents a legal requirement where none is described

options.text: Parties have survived by reorganising resources, so membership is a means rather than a condition of survival

questions.explanation: Parties whose membership collapsed have kept winning by concentrating money, staff and communication, so membership is a means of organisation rather than a condition of survival.
questions.hint: Ask what the parties did instead.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Correct the reading of catch-all strategies as a loss of principles
questions.stem: Patch note N-50: The draft treats a catch-all strategy as what a party does when it has lost its principles, and the fix must correct the reading.

options.text: Broadening can be a deliberate choice to hold a large coalition of voters rather than a symptom of loss
Adopting a catch-all strategy always follows the loss of a party's beliefs
options.misconception: asserts a necessary sequence that the note does not support

options.text: Catch-all parties exist only where no ideology has developed in the country
options.misconception: links the strategy to the absence of any ideology at all

options.text: A party that broadens must later abandon its candidates to stay consistent
options.misconception: invents a further consequence the strategy does not require

questions.explanation: The note describes broadening as a strategy for holding many voters together, so reading it as proof of lost principles mistakes a choice for a symptom. Nothing implies an absence of ideology.
questions.hint: Ask whether the change was chosen or suffered.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish the functions of a party from those of government
questions.stem: Repair R-43: The draft treats the functions of a party as those of government, and the reviewer wants the distinction written plainly.

answer.exemplar: The draft absorbs the party into the government, but the two have different jobs. A party is a durable organisation that aggregates interests, competes for votes, selects candidates, formulates programmes and mobilises voters, and it does these things whether or not it holds office. Government is the body that executes decisions, administers policy and answers to the legislature, and it exists only where a party or coalition has been entrusted with office. Treating the party as the government therefore erases the activity that happens precisely when the party is in opposition, which is the clearest evidence of what parties are for.

questions.explanation: Parties aggregate, compete and mobilise whether in or out of office, while government executes and administers once entrusted with power. Conflating them hides the opposition years.
questions.hint: Ask what a party does before it wins.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Apply the party system concept to a country mislabelled by vote share

stimulus.body: A research report describes a country as having a two-party system, citing the fact that two parties together took 71 per cent of the vote and that the election was conducted as a choice between two clear programmes. A smaller party took 22 per cent and doubled its seats, and a fourth party took 5 per cent and won a seat in the capital.

questions.stem: Common error E-63: The report uses a popular vote share to label the system, and the correction must apply the concept properly.

options.text: The country is a multi-party system, because three parties polled double figures
options.misconception: counts vote shares rather than assessing contender status

options.text: The label turns on which parties are viable contenders for office, not on how the vote divided
The two-party label is justified, since two parties together took a clear majority of the vote
options.misconception: equates a combined vote share with the pattern of politics

options.text: The label is justified, since the election offered a choice between two clear programmes
options.misconception: treats the ballot content as the definition of a system

questions.explanation: A large combined vote share says nothing about whether a third party is a plausible government, and here one has doubled its seats. The concept concerns who can plausibly win.
questions.hint: Ask who could plausibly form a government.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Classify a system with a dominant party and a credible opposition

stimulus.body: One party has held a majority in every election for two decades. Its main opponent runs credible local organisations, publishes a programme and has won more seats in each of the last three elections. Voters who support the opposition say they expect it to win within the decade, and the dominant party has not restricted registration or campaigning in any way recorded in the note.

questions.stem: Misreading R-51: The note describes a long-standing dominant party, and the correction must classify the system.

options.text: This is a one-party system, because the opposition's expectations show the result is fixed
options.misconception: reads voter expectations as institutional exclusion

options.text: The system cannot be classified, because opposition fortunes are still changing
options.misconception: claims opposition strength stops a system being classified

options.text: This is a competitive system with a dominant party, since credible alternatives remain free to compete
This is a one-party system, because a single party has held power for two decades
options.misconception: equates a long majority with the absence of alternatives

questions.explanation: A one-party system requires the exclusion of rivals, and the note records a credible opposition free to compete and growing. Long majority rule with real alternatives is dominance.
questions.hint: Ask whether rivals can win.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Balance the claim that two-party systems remove voters' manoeuvre
questions.stem: Confusion X-28: The draft says a two-party system leaves voters no room for manoeuvre, and the reviewer wants a balanced assessment.

options.text: A two-party system always produces identical programmes because competition is so intense
options.misconception: assumes intense competition removes all policy differences

options.text: Third parties are constitutionally impossible wherever two parties dominate
options.misconception: asserts a constitutional bar not mentioned anywhere

options.text: Voters in two-party systems systematically vote for the lesser evil rather than by preference
options.misconception: generalises a motive for voting to every case

options.text: Two parties can leave voters real choices within each programme, so limited choice is not the same as none

questions.explanation: Choosing between two parties is a choice with real differences of programme, and the number of parties is not the number of options inside each one. Voter motives need their own evidence.
questions.hint: Ask how many options each party offers.
